23 A sound wave is detected by a microphone that is connected to a cathode-ray oscilloscope
(CRO).
The screen of the CRO displays a waveform, as shown.
The time-base is set to 20 s div–1.
What is the frequency of the sound wave?
A
15 Hz
B
15 000 Hz
C
20 000 Hz
D
30 000 Hz

hints: Count the horizontal divisions for one complete sine wave on the CRO screen, for example from one peak to the next peak, using the $20 \, \mu\text{s div}^{-1}$ time-base.
Recall that the horizontal length of one cycle is the period $T$, where $T = \text{divisions per cycle} \times \text{time-base}$.
Convert $T$ from $\mu\text{s}$ to $\text{s}$ and then use $f = 1/T$ to get frequency in $\text{Hz}$.
walkthrough: Look at the horizontal axis of the CRO trace. One full cycle means the same point on the wave repeated, such as peak to peak.
Measure the cycle length: about 3 complete waves occupy about 10 horizontal divisions, so one cycle is $10/3 \approx 3.33$ divisions.
Multiply by the time-base to get the period: $T = 3.33 \times 20 \, \mu\text{s} \approx 66.7 \, \mu\text{s}$.

A.explanation: 15 Hz would need a period of about 0.067 s, which ignores the $\mu\text{s}$ time-base and is far too long for this trace.

B.explanation: A period of about $66.7 \, \mu\text{s}$ gives $f = 1/T \approx 15\,000 \, \text{Hz}$, matching the measured divisions.

C.explanation: 20 000 Hz would need $T = 50 \, \mu\text{s}$ or 2.5 divisions, which is shorter than the observed distance between successive peaks.

D.explanation: 30 000 Hz would need $T \approx 33 \, \mu\text{s}$, about half the true period, from counting a half-cycle as a full cycle.
